content: Nutritional assessment and growth monitoring are integral components of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy. The following details provide a comprehensive understanding of the processes and findings related to these aspects in IMCI-implementing countries: 1. Nutritional Assessment in IMCI: Nutritional assessment is conducted using anthropometric measurements such as weight-for-age (WFA), weight-for-height (WFH), height-for-age (HFA), and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC). These measurements are used to evaluate the nutritional status of children and identify malnutrition. In the current national IMCI chart booklets, these parameters are frequently employed to assess nutritional health. 2. Defining Acute Malnutrition: Acute malnutrition is identified using a combination of anthropometric measurements and clinical signs. The most commonly used clinical indicators include visible severe wasting and nutritional oedema. Among anthropometric measures, WFA, WFH, HFA, and MUAC are utilized. Visible severe wasting remains a widely used clinical sign in 39 countries. 3. Growth Monitoring Programs: A separate growth monitoring (GM) program, independent of IMCI, exists in 39 countries. These programs are often integrated with routine immunization schedules, child health cards, and community-based activities. Growth monitoring is also conducted during specific events such as National Nutrition Days or by healthcare workers at community levels, nurseries, and pediatric clinics. 4. Age Groups for Growth Monitoring: Growth monitoring is most commonly performed in children aged 0–60 months. This age group is prioritized due to the critical developmental period and the vulnerability of young children to growth faltering and malnutrition. 5. Anthropometric Measures for Growth Monitoring: The most frequently used anthropometric measure for growth monitoring is WFA, followed by WFH and HFA. These measures provide a comprehensive understanding of a child’s growth trajectory and nutritional status. 6. Coverage of Growth Monitoring: Data on the coverage of routine growth monitoring among children up to 12 months of age is available for 23 countries. However, there is a lack of data for the remaining countries, indicating gaps in monitoring and reporting systems. 7. Updates to IMCI Chart Booklets: The national IMCI chart booklets have been updated based on the 2014 generic chart booklet (trial version) in 19 countries. These updates ensure that the latest evidence-based practices are incorporated into the assessment and management of childhood illnesses. 8. Global Response and Regional Participation: A global survey conducted across six regions (AFRO, EMRO, Europe, PAHO, SEAR, and WPRO) received responses from 45 out of 101 countries (44.6%). The regional distribution of responses included 40% from AFRO, 13.3% from the Americas, 13.3% from EMRO, 8.9% from Europe, 2.2% from SEAR, and 22.2% from WPRO. In conclusion, growth monitoring and nutritional assessment are critical components of child health programs in IMCI-implementing countries. While significant progress has been made, there remain gaps in data availability, program coverage, and the integration of updated practices. Addressing these gaps is essential to improve child health outcomes globally.
